1. Project Architecture & Technical Overview

The EV Charging Demand Predictor is an educational full-stack web application developed for smart city EV charging infrastructure planning. The system analyzes historical charging records across city zones, predicts future demand using pure statistical algorithms in Java, contrasts projected demand against operational station capacities, identifies under-served zones using a Priority Queue, and recommends precise station expansions.

1.1 System Architecture Diagram

[ React 18 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS Frontend ] │ ▼ (REST API / Axios JSON Calls) [ Spring Boot 3 Controller Layer (@RestController) ] │ ▼ (Service Layer & OOP Engine) [ Java Statistical Forecasting Engine (SMA + WMA + LR) ] │ ▼ (PriorityQueue Heap Ranking & What-If Simulation) [ Spring Data JPA / Hibernate ORM ] │ ▼ (TCP 3306) [ MySQL Relational Database (ev_charging_db) ]

2. Mathematical Formulation of Forecasting Models

The system computes daily EV session demand across configurable rolling windows ($N$) and projects predictions over forward horizons ($h = 1 dots H$). All three models produce synchronized multi-day horizons combined via an ensemble average.

2.1 Simple Moving Average (SMA)

Averages the latest $N$ values using recursive rolling progression:

\text{SMA}_{t+1} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} y_{t-i}

2.2 Weighted Moving Average (WMA)

Assigns linearly increasing integer weights $1, 2, \dots, N$ giving highest priority to recent demand:

\text{WMA}_{t+1} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (i \times y_{t-N+i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} i} = \frac{2 \sum_{i=1}^{N} (i \times y_{t-N+i})}{N(N+1)}

2.3 Ordinary Least Squares Linear Regression (LR)

Fits slope ($m$) and y-intercept ($c$) across historical index positions $x = 1 \dots N$:

m = \frac{N \sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{N \sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2}, \quad c = \frac{\sum y - m \sum x}{N}, \quad y(x) = mx + c

2.4 Final Ensemble Forecast & Demand Gap Analysis

\text{Final Forecast}_d = \frac{\text{SMA}_d + \text{WMA}_d + \text{LR}_d}{3} \\ \text{Demand Gap} = \left( \frac{1}{H} \sum_{d=1}^{H} \text{Final Forecast}_d \right) - \sum \text{Operational Station Capacity}

4. Examiner Viva Voce Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is this project built with statistical forecasting rather than Deep Learning / Machine Learning?

Answer: In urban planning and critical decision-support systems, explainability and reproducibility are paramount. Statistical models like Simple Moving Average, Weighted Moving Average, and Ordinary Least Squares Linear Regression have transparent mathematical formulations, zero risk of overfitting on modest dataset sizes, execute in sub-millisecond time on Java virtual machines without expensive GPUs, and provide verifiable forecasts that examiners and city engineers can audit directly.

Q2: How does the application ensure that Linear Regression and Moving Averages generate the same forecast horizon?

Answer: All models inherit from PredictionModel and implement the forecast(double[] historicalData, int horizon) method. Moving Average models (SMA and WMA) project future days recursively by computing the prediction for day $t+1$ and rolling that value back into the window to compute day $t+2$. Linear Regression calculates the linear regression coefficients ($m$ and $c$) across the $N$-point window and projects future days directly using 1-based indexing ($x = N + 1, N + 2, \dots, N + h$), ensuring all three series produce identical array lengths.

Q3: How is Polymorphism demonstrated in the charging station calculations?

Answer: The abstract class Station defines public abstract double calculateChargingTime(Vehicle vehicle). In FastChargingStation, charging operates at 90% efficiency below 80% State of Charge (SoC) and throttles down to 40% above 80% SoC to protect battery health. In SlowChargingStation, efficiency is constant at 85%. In SolarChargingStation, efficiency dynamically adjusts based on peak sunlight hours (10:00–16:00 at 95% efficiency, 45% during off-peak).

Q4: Why does the Priority Queue filter out zones with negative or zero demand gaps?

Answer: A negative demand gap means existing station capacity exceeds predicted demand (status ADEQUATE). Since municipal budgets for new EV chargers are limited, allocating funds to adequately served zones would be wasteful. Filtering by $\text{Demand Gap} > 0$ guarantees that only sectors suffering from charging deficits enter the PriorityQueue for expansion ranking.
